destinations.title: Access control
destinations.def: Rules and technical controls that determine who or what can reach a system, resource, or action, and with what level of authority.
destinations.plain: Think of it as deciding which doors an account or AI agent can open, and whether it can only look, make changes, or take full control.
destinations.why: Agents become much riskier when they can reach sensitive data, production systems, email, payments, or code. Limiting access can contain damage even when the model behaves unexpectedly.

sections.title: Access control
sections.def: The overall system for deciding and enforcing access.

sections.title: Permissions
sections.def: The specific allowed actions or resources granted to an identity, such as read, write, delete, or publish.

sections.title: Privilege escalation
sections.def: Gaining more authority than an account or process was supposed to have.

sections.title: Root access
sections.def: Administrator-level control over a Unix-like computer, with power to change essentially anything on that machine.

destinations.title: Advanced packaging
destinations.def: Chip-manufacturing techniques that combine processors, memory, and other components in tightly integrated packages.
destinations.plain: Instead of improving only the tiny transistors inside a chip, manufacturers also improve how multiple chip pieces are connected and stacked together.
destinations.why: AI systems move enormous amounts of data between processors and memory. Better packaging can raise performance and efficiency even when transistor improvements slow.

destinations.title: Agent identity
destinations.def: The digital identity an AI agent uses when it authenticates to tools, services, or data.
destinations.plain: An agent often needs an account, credential, or service identity just like a person or software program does. That identity determines what systems recognize it as and what it can do.
destinations.why: A shared or overpowered identity makes it hard to limit, audit, or revoke an agent. Separate identities make permissions and accountability clearer.

destinations.title: Agent platforms
destinations.def: Software environments that package models with tools, memory, integrations, interfaces, and controls so AI agents can perform work.
destinations.plain: The model is the brain-like component; the platform or wrapper is the surrounding product that gives it access to files, apps, workflows, and users.
destinations.why: Much of the real-world value and risk of AI now comes from this surrounding layer, not from the underlying model alone.

sections.title: Agent platform
sections.def: A broader environment for building, running, managing, or connecting agents.

sections.title: AI wrapper
sections.def: A product layer built around an existing model or API to provide a specific interface or workflow; it may be much thinner than a full agent platform.

destinations.title: Agent security
destinations.def: Security controls that limit what AI agents can access, do, and affect when they operate.
destinations.plain: Because an agent can take actions, security is not only about blocking bad words. It is about restricting its tools, network, credentials, files, and ability to change the outside world.
destinations.why: Prompt instructions can fail. Technical limits on reach and authority reduce how much damage an agent can cause when it makes a mistake or pursues a goal too aggressively.

sections.title: Agent security
sections.def: The broad practice of protecting systems from risks created by agents and protecting agents from malicious inputs or environments. In Prompted’s “agent safety” passages, this is the intended sense: security engineering around credentials, tools, network reach, execution boundaries, and other controls on what an agent can actually do.

sections.title: Agent containment
sections.def: The narrower problem of keeping an agent inside intended technical boundaries, such as a sandbox, limited network, or restricted set of tools.

destinations.title: Agent workflows
destinations.def: Ways of structuring AI agents so they can carry out multi-step work, sometimes across time or repeated sessions.
destinations.plain: Instead of answering once, an agent can follow a sequence of steps, wait, resume, use tools, and keep working toward an outcome.
destinations.why: Longer-running workflows can automate more useful work, but they also create more places for errors, stale assumptions, or unsafe actions to compound.

sections.title: Agentic workflow
sections.def: A workflow in which an AI agent chooses or executes multiple steps toward a goal rather than merely producing one response.

sections.title: Persistent agent
sections.def: An agent designed to remain available or continue operating across sessions or over time instead of disappearing after one interaction.

destinations.title: AI accelerators
destinations.def: Specialized computer hardware designed to perform the large matrix calculations used heavily in AI.
destinations.plain: These chips are built to run AI math faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU.
destinations.why: Accelerators largely determine how expensive and fast training and running modern AI can be.

sections.title: AI accelerator
sections.def: The broad category of specialized chips used for AI workloads, including GPUs, TPUs, and other custom designs.

sections.title: Inference accelerator
sections.def: An accelerator optimized specifically for running trained models and producing outputs, rather than primarily for training them.

destinations.title: AI agents
destinations.def: AI systems that can pursue goals by choosing steps and using tools or software, rather than only returning a single answer.
destinations.plain: An agent is AI with some ability to act: it might browse, edit files, run code, call apps, or hand work to other agents.
destinations.why: The more an AI system can act independently, the more useful it can become—and the more important permissions, monitoring, and human checkpoints become.

sections.title: AI agent
sections.def: A specific AI system that can take actions or execute multi-step work toward a goal. In Prompted, plain “agent” or “agents” refers to this concept when the surrounding context is AI.

sections.title: Agentic AI
sections.def: AI designed around agent-like behavior: planning, tool use, delegation, persistence, or autonomous execution. It describes the style or capability, not necessarily one particular agent.

destinations.title: AI governance
destinations.def: The structures, rules, processes, roles, and controls used to direct and oversee AI systems and the organizations that build or deploy them.
destinations.plain: Governance answers who has authority and accountability, how an AI organization or program is structured, what testing or access rules apply, what evidence must be kept, and when people or regulators can intervene.
destinations.why: As AI moves into consequential work, organizations and governments increasingly require controls that are operational and auditable, not just broad principles.

sections.title: AI governance
sections.def: The broad oversight of AI development and use, including the institutions and organizations responsible for it.

sections.title: Frontier governance
sections.def: Governance aimed specifically at the most capable frontier models or labs, where national-security or catastrophic-risk concerns may justify extra controls.

destinations.title: AI infrastructure
destinations.def: The computing, networking, data-center, power, cloud, and software foundations needed to train and run AI systems.
destinations.plain: It is the machinery underneath the visible AI product: chips, servers, networks, storage, electricity, and the systems that keep them working.
destinations.why: Infrastructure has become a major competitive constraint because advanced AI needs huge amounts of capital, compute, power, and capacity.

destinations.title: AI models
destinations.def: A trained computational system that has learned patterns from data and uses those patterns to produce predictions, decisions, or generated output.
destinations.plain: In Prompted, “model” usually means the learned AI engine itself—not the app, agent, framework, or business structure wrapped around it.
destinations.why: Model capability, cost, size, access, and release terms shape what products can do, but the same model can behave very differently depending on how it is deployed and controlled.

sections.title: AI model
sections.def: The general Prompted term for an AI model; qualifying plain “model” and “models” references use this meaning unless the text is discussing a non-AI sense.

sections.title: LLM
sections.def: Large language model: a model trained on large amounts of text and related data to understand and generate language.

sections.title: Foundation model
sections.def: A broadly trained model that can be adapted or used across many downstream tasks rather than being built for only one narrow job.

sections.title: Generative AI
sections.def: Artificial intelligence that produces content such as text, images, audio or video using patterns learned from data.
sections.plain: It creates an output in response to an input, rather than only assigning a label or predicting a number. Generated content is not necessarily accurate or original.
sections.why: Adoption figures and school restrictions may concern content-generating tools specifically, not every kind of AI.

destinations.title: AI reasoning
destinations.def: AI reasoning is the process of an AI system working through a problem using intermediate deliberation; a reasoning trace records or exposes that work, while an effort level controls how much deliberation the system is allowed to use.
destinations.plain: The model can do more than jump straight to an answer: it can work through alternatives or subproblems first. A product may also give users a reasoning dial, effort toggle, or thinking level that trades speed and cost against how much work the model does before responding.
destinations.why: Reasoning capability affects difficult tasks, while the amount of reasoning used can materially change latency, price, and reliability.

sections.title: AI reasoning
sections.def: The general act or capability of an AI working through a problem. It is distinct from a “reasoning model,” which is a model category; parent/child overlap is allowed when the corpus explicitly expresses both.

sections.title: Reasoning trace
sections.def: A recorded or exposed sequence representing intermediate reasoning steps or internal problem-solving activity; it is not the reasoning capability itself.

sections.title: Effort level
sections.def: A user- or system-selectable setting that controls how much reasoning work a model spends on a request, often trading more time or compute for a stronger attempt. Prompted uses equivalent phrases such as reasoning dial, thinking effort, effort toggle, and thinking levels.

destinations.title: AI safety and alignment
destinations.def: The field of reducing the chance that AI systems cause unintended or unacceptable harm and keeping their behavior compatible with intended goals and constraints.
destinations.plain: Safety is the broad risk problem. Alignment is the narrower question of whether the system’s goals and behavior actually match what people intended.
destinations.why: More capable systems can create bigger consequences when they misunderstand a goal, are misused, or pursue the wrong objective.

sections.title: AI safety
sections.def: The broad effort to prevent or reduce harmful AI outcomes.

sections.title: AI alignment
sections.def: The effort to make an AI system’s behavior and objectives reliably match intended human goals and constraints.

sections.title: Misalignment
sections.def: A mismatch between what people intend and what an AI system is optimizing for or doing.

sections.title: Catastrophic risk
sections.def: Risk of harm at an extreme scale, such as very large loss of life, severe societal disruption, or other consequences far beyond ordinary product failures.

destinations.title: AI sovereignty
destinations.def: The ability of a country or organization to control where its AI systems, data, infrastructure, and dependencies reside and who governs them.
destinations.plain: Sovereignty means not having every important AI capability depend on a foreign provider, foreign law, or infrastructure outside your control.
destinations.why: Governments and regulated organizations increasingly care about where models and data run because access can be restricted by law, geopolitics, or vendor decisions.

sections.title: AI sovereignty
sections.def: The broad goal of retaining strategic control over AI capability, data, infrastructure, and policy.

sections.title: Sovereign hosting
sections.def: Hosting AI systems and data inside a specified jurisdiction or trusted national environment so local control and legal requirements can be maintained.

destinations.title: AI stack
destinations.def: The layers of technology that combine to deliver an AI product, from infrastructure and models up through applications.
destinations.plain: Think of a stack as the chain underneath what the user sees: chips and cloud at the bottom, models in the middle, and apps and workflows on top.
destinations.why: Companies compete at different layers, and control of several layers can create cost, distribution, or lock-in advantages.

sections.title: AI stack
sections.def: The overall layered technology chain used to build and deliver AI.

sections.title: Full stack
sections.def: Operating or controlling multiple major layers of that chain rather than only one component.

sections.title: Application layer
sections.def: The user-facing software and workflows built on top of models and infrastructure.

sections.title: Model layer
sections.def: The part of the stack where the AI models themselves are provided, selected, or run.

destinations.title: Algorithmic collusion
destinations.def: Coordination between competing algorithms that produces collusive outcomes, such as higher prices, even without an explicit human agreement.
destinations.plain: If automated pricing systems learn that competing aggressively hurts both sides, they may settle into behavior that resembles a cartel.
destinations.why: It creates an antitrust problem because harmful coordination could emerge from optimization rather than a traditional secret deal.

destinations.title: API
destinations.def: Application programming interface: a defined way for one piece of software to request data or actions from another.
destinations.plain: An AI API lets developers send a model input from their own software and receive the model’s output without using the provider’s consumer app.
destinations.why: APIs are how many AI products are built and priced, and changing API access, limits, or terms can directly affect downstream companies.

destinations.title: Autonomy
destinations.def: The degree to which a system can choose and carry out actions without a person directing every step.
destinations.plain: More autonomy means the system can decide what to do next on its own for longer stretches.
destinations.why: Autonomy can increase productivity, but mistakes can propagate further before a human notices.

sections.title: Autonomy
sections.def: The general property or degree of independent action.

sections.title: Autonomous system
sections.def: A particular system designed to sense, decide, or act with limited ongoing human direction.

destinations.title: Behind-the-meter power
destinations.def: Electric generation or storage located on the customer’s side of the utility meter and used directly by that site.
destinations.plain: A data center can put power generation or batteries on-site instead of relying entirely on electricity delivered through the public grid.
destinations.why: AI data centers need enormous amounts of reliable power, so behind-the-meter arrangements can speed capacity or reduce grid constraints, while shifting costs and risks in different ways.

destinations.title: Benchmarks
destinations.def: A standardized test or task used to compare how well AI systems perform.
destinations.plain: Benchmarks are scoreboards for models. Benchmarking means running or comparing systems on these tests. They are useful only if the test actually measures the desired capability and the model has not effectively seen the answers beforehand.
destinations.why: Launch claims often depend on benchmark scores, so test design and contamination determine how much those numbers should be trusted.

sections.title: Benchmark
sections.def: A standardized test or measurement used to compare AI systems; “benchmarking” is the process of running or comparing systems on such tests.

sections.title: Test contamination
sections.def: When benchmark material leaks into training or development, making a score less informative because the model may have seen the test or close variants before.

destinations.title: Browser agents
destinations.def: An AI agent that can operate a web browser to navigate sites, read pages, fill forms, click controls, or complete web-based tasks.
destinations.plain: Instead of only telling you what to click, a browser agent can click and type for you.
destinations.why: Browser access gives agents a powerful bridge into real services, so credentials, permissions, and confirmation before consequential actions matter.

destinations.title: Capability thresholds
destinations.def: A defined level of AI capability that triggers a different safety, security, access, or governance response.
destinations.plain: Organizations can set lines such as: below this capability, normal controls apply; above it, stronger testing or restrictions turn on.
destinations.why: Thresholds convert vague concern into operational rules, but the consequence depends on how the threshold is measured and enforced.

sections.title: Capability threshold
sections.def: Any predefined capability level used to trigger a policy or control.

sections.title: Critical threshold
sections.def: A higher-severity threshold—often a named tier in a lab’s safety framework—where the capability is serious enough to require substantially stronger safeguards. The exact test depends on the framework using the label.

destinations.title: CapEx
destinations.def: Capital expenditures: money spent on long-lived assets such as data centers, servers, chips, buildings, or power infrastructure.
destinations.plain: CapEx is spending to build or buy the physical capacity a company expects to use for years, rather than an ordinary day-to-day operating expense.
destinations.why: AI has pushed CapEx sharply higher because leading companies are building enormous computing and power capacity, making returns on that investment a central business question.

destinations.title: Classifiers
destinations.def: A model or system that assigns an input to a category or score, such as safe/unsafe, spam/not spam, or topic labels.
destinations.plain: A classifier is a specialized judge: it looks at something and labels it according to learned rules or patterns.
destinations.why: AI products often use classifiers around larger models to detect risky requests, moderate output, route traffic, or enforce policy.

destinations.title: Cloud and hyperscalers
destinations.def: Cloud computing delivers rented computing resources over networks; hyperscalers are the very large providers capable of supplying cloud infrastructure at enormous scale.
destinations.plain: Instead of owning every server, companies can rent capacity from providers such as the major global clouds. Multi-cloud means a product or workload uses or is distributed through more than one cloud provider.
destinations.why: Frontier AI needs huge and reliable capacity, so cloud relationships can shape access, costs, bargaining power, and resilience.

sections.title: Hyperscaler
sections.def: A cloud or infrastructure company operating data centers and computing services at exceptionally large scale.

sections.title: Multi-cloud
sections.def: An arrangement where a product, workload, or organization uses or is distributed across multiple cloud providers rather than depending on only one.

destinations.title: Coding agents
destinations.def: An AI agent specialized in software-development work such as reading code, editing files, running tests, debugging, and using developer tools.
destinations.plain: It is more than code autocomplete: a coding agent can take a programming goal and carry out multiple steps inside a development environment.
destinations.why: Coding agents are one of the clearest areas where AI is moving from suggestions to action, raising both productivity and security questions.

destinations.title: Compute
destinations.def: The processing capacity used to perform computational work, especially the chip time needed to train or run AI models.
destinations.plain: In AI stories, “compute” usually means how much high-performance computing power is available or consumed.
destinations.why: Compute is expensive and supply-constrained, so access to it can determine who can train frontier models or serve them at scale.

destinations.title: Connectors and MCP
destinations.def: Ways for AI systems to connect to outside tools, data sources, and services.
destinations.plain: A connector links an AI product to something it could not otherwise reach. MCP is a standardized protocol designed so AI applications can connect to tools and context through a common interface.
destinations.why: Connections make agents much more useful, but they also expand what the AI can access and therefore what must be authenticated, permissioned, and secured.

sections.title: Connector
sections.def: A specific integration that gives an AI system access to an external app, data source, or tool.

sections.title: MCP
sections.def: Model Context Protocol: an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools, resources, and contextual data through a standardized client-server interface.

destinations.title: Context windows
destinations.def: The amount of information a model can consider at one time when processing a request.
destinations.plain: The context window is the model’s working space for your prompt, conversation, documents, tool results, and other supplied text or data.
destinations.why: A larger window lets a model handle longer material, but size alone does not guarantee it will use every part reliably or cheaply.

destinations.title: Contingent backstops
destinations.def: A backup commitment that becomes financially active only if specified risks or shortfalls occur.
destinations.plain: It is not cash paid upfront. A backstop is a promise to absorb defined losses if something such as lease payments, power obligations, or asset values fail to meet expectations.
destinations.why: In giant AI infrastructure deals, backstops can move risk between companies and make projects financeable without being the same thing as direct investment.

destinations.title: Cost per task
destinations.def: The total cost required for an AI system to successfully complete a useful unit of work.
destinations.plain: Price per token tells you what each model call costs; cost per task asks what the finished outcome cost after all calls, retries, tools, and failures.
destinations.why: A cheap model that needs many attempts can be more expensive than a pricier model that succeeds once, so task economics are often more useful than headline API prices.

destinations.title: Credentials
destinations.def: Information or devices used to prove an identity and gain authorized access to a system.
destinations.plain: Credentials answer “who are you?” A password, token, passkey, or physical security key can all play that role, but they work differently.
destinations.why: Agents and connected AI systems often need credentials to act in real software. How those credentials are issued, stored, limited, and revoked determines what the AI can reach.

sections.title: Credential
sections.def: The general proof or secret used to authenticate an identity or authorize access.

sections.title: Passkey
sections.def: A phishing-resistant login credential based on public-key cryptography, usually unlocked through a user’s device and designed to replace passwords.

sections.title: Security key
sections.def: A separate physical hardware device, often USB/NFC, that stores cryptographic credentials and can be required for login. A security key can hold passkeys, but the hardware device and the passkey credential are not the same thing.

destinations.title: Custom silicon
destinations.def: Chips designed by or for a particular company or workload instead of relying only on general off-the-shelf processors.
destinations.plain: A company can build silicon tuned for the calculations, power use, or systems it cares about most.
destinations.why: Custom chips can lower AI costs, improve performance, and reduce dependence on outside suppliers, which is why major AI and cloud companies invest heavily in them.

destinations.title: Data governance and retention
destinations.def: Policies and controls governing what data is collected, stored, accessed, used, shared, and deleted.
destinations.plain: Data governance is the rulebook; retention is how long data stays; PII is information that can identify a person.
destinations.why: AI systems often process sensitive inputs and logs. Weak rules around data can create privacy, legal, security, and procurement problems even when the model itself works well.

sections.title: Data governance
sections.def: The broader system of rules, ownership, controls, and accountability for data.

sections.title: Data retention
sections.def: The policy or practice determining how long data, prompts, logs, or other records are kept before deletion or archival.

sections.title: PII
sections.def: Personally identifiable information: information that identifies, or can reasonably be linked to, a specific person.

destinations.title: Data poisoning
destinations.def: Deliberately corrupting training or reference data so an AI system learns harmful behavior or produces manipulated results.
destinations.plain: An attacker puts bad examples into the information the model learns from or relies on, hoping those examples change what it later does.
destinations.why: AI systems depend heavily on data, so poisoning can create hidden vulnerabilities that are difficult to notice until the model is used.

destinations.title: Deployment
destinations.def: The process and environment for putting an AI system into real use.
destinations.plain: Building or training a model is not the same as running it for users. Deployment covers where it runs, how it is connected, scaled, monitored, and operated.
destinations.why: Many important AI tradeoffs—cost, privacy, reliability, and control—appear at deployment time.

sections.title: Deployment
sections.def: Putting and operating an AI system in a real environment; Prompted also uses related forms such as deploy, deployed, and deployments when they clearly refer to this process.

sections.title: Hybrid deployment
sections.def: A setup that splits AI workloads across more than one environment, such as cloud plus on-premises systems.

sections.title: On-prem
sections.def: On-premises: running systems on computing infrastructure controlled at the organization’s own site or facilities rather than entirely in a public cloud.

destinations.title: Digital Markets Act
destinations.def: A European Union law that imposes special obligations on designated large digital “gatekeepers” to keep certain core platform markets fair and contestable.
destinations.plain: The DMA can require dominant platforms to change how they distribute services, treat rivals, or connect users to competing products.
destinations.why: AI assistants increasingly depend on operating systems, app stores, browsers, and messaging platforms, so DMA enforcement can directly shape which AI products reach users.

destinations.title: Domain-specialized models
destinations.def: An AI model designed or adapted for a particular field, industry, or type of work rather than broad general use.
destinations.plain: Instead of trying to do everything, a specialized model focuses on a domain such as law, medicine, coding, finance, or scientific data.
destinations.why: Specialization can improve cost or performance on important tasks, but it can also narrow flexibility and make domain-specific evaluation more important.

destinations.title: Dual-use AI
destinations.def: Technology that has legitimate beneficial uses but can also be used to cause harm.
destinations.plain: The same AI capability that helps defenders find software flaws can help attackers exploit them; the capability itself is not exclusively good or bad.
destinations.why: Dual-use capability makes release and access decisions difficult because restricting harmful use can also limit valuable use.

destinations.title: Embodied AI
destinations.def: AI that perceives and acts through a physical body or machine, such as a robot, vehicle, or laboratory device.
destinations.plain: Embodied AI connects software intelligence to sensors and physical actions in the real world.
destinations.why: Errors can have physical consequences, so safety requires controlling not only model outputs but also what machinery is allowed to execute.

destinations.title: EU AI Act
destinations.def: The European Union’s comprehensive legal framework for AI, which regulates systems differently according to their role and level of risk. This page also explains related “general-purpose” and “high-risk” language that Prompted sometimes uses outside the Act’s formal categories.
destinations.plain: The AI Act does not treat every AI system the same. Some uses face specific obligations, and providers of broadly capable general-purpose models have separate requirements. But “general-purpose” can also describe an AI assistant meant to handle many tasks, and other laws can define their own high-risk AI categories.
destinations.why: Companies serving EU users may face documentation, transparency, risk-management, and other duties depending on what they provide and how the AI is used; similar labels in other laws do not automatically carry the EU Act’s exact definition.

sections.title: EU AI Act
sections.def: The EU-wide AI law itself. Prompted excludes references to unrelated laws such as the Colorado AI Act from this term.

sections.title: GPAI
sections.def: Under the EU AI Act, a general-purpose AI model is a broadly capable model that can perform many different tasks and be integrated into many downstream systems. Prompted also uses broader descriptive forms such as “general-purpose AI,” “general-purpose model,” and “general-purpose assistants”; those phrases describe broad-purpose capability and are not automatically a statement that the product is legally classified as a GPAI model under the Act.

sections.title: High-risk AI
sections.def: A regulatory category for AI uses a law treats as especially consequential and therefore subjects to stricter requirements. The exact category depends on the law. Under the EU AI Act it includes specified uses where failures can significantly affect safety or fundamental rights; other laws, including Colorado’s, can use their own high-risk definitions.

destinations.title: Evaluation
destinations.def: A structured assessment of an AI system, its behavior, or an AI-related program or use.
destinations.plain: An evaluation, often shortened to “eval,” sets up a test, pilot, or measurement process and asks what the AI or the program around it actually does. Model evals may test capability, safety, or reliability; real-world pilots can test whether an AI product or intervention works in practice.
destinations.why: AI performance can change by task, setup, and test design, so decisions about access, deployment, procurement, or policy often depend on how evaluations are run and who verifies them.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.def: The broad structured-assessment concept in Prompted’s AI contexts. “Evaluation,” “evaluations,” “eval,” and “evals” qualify when they concern AI systems, AI programs, or their real-world use; ordinary source-evaluation language does not.

sections.title: Independent eval
sections.def: An evaluation or testing process run or verified by a party meaningfully separate from the model developer, reducing the risk that the developer shaped the test in its own favor.

sections.title: Double-blind eval
sections.def: In Prompted’s historical use, an evaluation whose questions or test materials were hidden from the model-development team in advance. The phrase does not imply that the evaluators themselves were blind unless a source specifically says so.

sections.title: Eval harness
sections.def: The software framework that presents tests to models, controls the environment, records outputs, and computes or organizes evaluation results.

destinations.title: Export controls
destinations.def: Government restrictions on the export or foreign transfer of specified technology, products, software, or access for national-security or foreign-policy reasons.
destinations.plain: Export controls can limit who in another country may receive advanced chips, model access, technical know-how, or other sensitive capabilities.
destinations.why: AI competition is increasingly shaped by law as well as engineering, and access rules can change who is able to train, run, or use frontier systems.

sections.title: Export controls
sections.def: The general restrictions governing transfers across national borders or to foreign persons.

sections.title: Extraterritorial controls
sections.def: Rules that reach transactions or actors outside the regulating country, for example because controlled technology, persons, or supply chains create a legal connection.

destinations.title: Fair use
destinations.def: A U.S. copyright doctrine that can allow limited use of copyrighted material without the copyright owner’s permission after weighing the circumstances of the use.
destinations.plain: Fair use is not a blanket exemption. Courts balance factors including the purpose of the use, the nature of the work, how much was used, and the effect on the market.
destinations.why: AI training and output lawsuits often turn in part on whether particular copying qualifies as fair use, and different facts can produce different answers.

destinations.title: FERPA
destinations.def: The U.S. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a federal law protecting the privacy of student education records at covered schools and institutions.
destinations.plain: FERPA gives eligible students and parents certain rights over education records and limits when schools may disclose personally identifiable information from those records.
destinations.why: Schools evaluating AI tools need to understand what student data leaves institutional systems, who receives it, and whether sharing complies with education-privacy obligations.

destinations.title: Fine-tuning and distillation
destinations.def: Methods for adapting or compressing an existing model after its main training.
destinations.plain: Fine-tuning further trains a model on additional targeted data so it behaves better for a task or domain. Distillation trains a smaller or different model to imitate useful behavior from a stronger model.
destinations.why: Both techniques can change capability and economics without paying the full cost of training a frontier model from scratch.

sections.title: Fine-tuning
sections.def: Additional training of an existing model on selected data to adapt its behavior or performance.

sections.title: Model distillation
sections.def: Training one model using outputs or behavior from another model as teaching signal, often to transfer capability into a smaller, cheaper, or independently controlled model.

destinations.title: Formal verification and proof checking
destinations.def: Methods for checking whether a claim, program, proof, or system satisfies precisely stated rules using formal logic or automated verification.
destinations.plain: Instead of trusting that an answer looks right, formal methods try to prove or mechanically check that it follows defined mathematical or logical rules.
destinations.why: AI-generated code and mathematics can be persuasive but wrong. Verification and proof checking can catch some classes of errors, although they verify the formal claim—not whether a person understood it or whether the chosen assumptions were good.

sections.title: Formal verification
sections.def: Using mathematical methods to prove that a system or result satisfies specified properties.

sections.title: Proof checking
sections.def: Mechanically verifying that a proposed formal proof follows the permitted rules and reaches the stated conclusion.

destinations.title: Forward-deployed engineers
destinations.def: Engineers who work directly inside or alongside a customer organization to adapt technology to that customer’s real systems and workflows.
destinations.plain: Instead of handing over software and leaving, a forward-deployed engineer helps integrate it, reshape processes, solve edge cases, and get measurable results in the field.
destinations.why: As AI value shifts from demos to implementation, these roles are becoming central to enterprise adoption and a major source of near-term AI jobs.

destinations.title: Free cash flow
destinations.def: Cash generated by a business after paying operating costs and the capital spending needed to maintain or grow the business.
destinations.plain: It is roughly the cash left over after the company runs itself and funds major investments.
destinations.why: AI infrastructure is extremely capital-intensive, so investors watch whether companies can fund expansion while still producing cash rather than relying indefinitely on outside financing.

destinations.title: Frontier labs
destinations.def: Organizations operating at or near the leading edge of general-purpose AI capability.
destinations.plain: A frontier lab is a company or research organization building the most capable models of its time, such as the major labs Prompted follows each week.
destinations.why: These labs shape the technical frontier and increasingly influence policy, infrastructure spending, safety standards, and the products built downstream.

destinations.title: Frontier models
destinations.def: An AI model at or near the current leading edge of broadly useful capability.
destinations.plain: “Frontier” is relative to the state of the art, not a permanent technical category. A frontier model today can become ordinary as the field advances.
destinations.why: The strongest models often receive extra scrutiny because they can enable valuable new work and potentially more serious misuse or failures.

destinations.title: Full-duplex AI
destinations.def: A conversational AI design that can listen and speak at the same time instead of forcing strict turn-taking.
destinations.plain: Like a natural phone conversation, the system can hear an interruption while it is talking and respond without waiting for a full stop.
destinations.why: Full-duplex systems make voice AI feel faster and more natural and can let background reasoning or tools run while the spoken interaction continues.

destinations.title: GPU
destinations.def: Graphics processing unit: a massively parallel processor originally developed for graphics and now widely used for AI calculations.
destinations.plain: GPUs can perform many similar mathematical operations at once, which makes them well suited to training and running neural networks.
destinations.why: Supply of high-end GPUs, their cost, and access to large clusters have become central constraints in the AI buildout.

destinations.title: Grounding and hallucinations
destinations.def: Grounding anchors an AI system’s output or behavior to external source material or real-world data; a hallucination is content the AI presents as supported or true when it is not.
destinations.plain: Grounding gives the model something concrete outside its own generated guesses to work from, such as a document, database, search result, image, map, or other real-world reference. Hallucination is when the model fills gaps with invented or unsupported material.
destinations.why: Grounding can make answers, generated environments, and other AI outputs more faithful to the sources or reality they are supposed to represent.

sections.title: Grounding
sections.def: Connecting AI output or behavior to specific external evidence, source material, or real-world data so it stays anchored to what it is supposed to represent.

sections.title: Hallucination
sections.def: A model-generated statement, citation, detail, or claim that is false or unsupported but is presented confidently as if it were valid.

destinations.title: Guardrails and refusals
destinations.def: Controls that restrict, filter, or block AI behavior judged unsafe, disallowed, or outside policy.
destinations.plain: A guardrail is the broad protective boundary. A refusal is the model declining a request. A safety filter is a technical check that can block or alter input or output.
destinations.why: These controls reduce misuse risk, but they can be bypassed or over-trigger, so serious security cannot depend on them alone.

sections.title: Guardrail
sections.def: A broad rule or technical control intended to keep an AI system within acceptable behavior.

sections.title: Refusal
sections.def: A model declining to comply with a request or part of a request because it conflicts with policy, safety rules, or capability limits.

sections.title: Safety filter
sections.def: A technical component that detects and blocks, reroutes, or modifies content judged risky or disallowed.

destinations.title: HBM and VRAM
destinations.def: High-speed memory used close to AI processors to hold data the chips need while computing.
destinations.plain: HBM is specialized high-bandwidth memory packaged very close to accelerators; VRAM is the memory available to a graphics or accelerator processor for its active workloads.
destinations.why: Modern models move so much data that memory capacity and bandwidth can limit speed, model size, and the number of users a system can serve.

sections.title: HBM
sections.def: High-bandwidth memory: stacked, very high-throughput memory commonly paired with advanced AI accelerators.

sections.title: VRAM
sections.def: Video memory: memory directly available to a GPU or similar accelerator for model weights, activations, and working data while a workload runs.

destinations.title: Human oversight
destinations.def: Ways of keeping people or accountable institutions responsible for consequential AI decisions, access, systems, or actions.
destinations.plain: Human oversight means people remain able to supervise, intervene, or take responsibility. Approval is explicit authorization before an AI action, system, access grant, or output is allowed to proceed or be used; review is inspection of AI work or decisions before or after execution.
destinations.why: When AI can alter real systems or enter consequential workflows, human checkpoints can prevent irreversible mistakes and make accountability clearer.

sections.title: Human approval
sections.def: Explicit authorization by a person or accountable institution before an AI action, access grant, system, or consequential output is allowed to proceed or be used.

sections.title: Human review
sections.def: A person inspects AI work or decisions for correctness, risk, or appropriateness; it may occur before or after execution.

sections.title: Human oversight
sections.def: The broader arrangement in which humans supervise, govern, intervene in, and remain accountable for an AI system.

destinations.title: Incident reporting
destinations.def: A requirement or process for documenting and notifying relevant parties when a significant AI failure, misuse event, security breach, or other defined incident occurs.
destinations.plain: It is the AI equivalent of having a formal “something went wrong” reporting path rather than discovering problems informally.
destinations.why: Timely incident reporting helps users, regulators, and vendors respond to harm, learn from failures, and detect patterns across systems.

destinations.title: Inference
destinations.def: Running a trained AI model to produce outputs from new inputs.
destinations.plain: Training is when the model learns; inference is when you use what it learned. Every chatbot answer or model API response is an inference workload.
destinations.why: Inference happens at huge scale and drives much of AI’s ongoing cost, latency, and hardware demand.

sections.title: Inference
sections.def: The act of running a trained model to generate a prediction or output.

sections.title: Inference caching
sections.def: Reusing previously computed work from earlier or repeated input so a request needs less new computation. An input-cache hit means part of the incoming request matches cached input and can be reused, which is why providers can process or price that input more cheaply.

sections.title: Speculative decoding
sections.def: An inference technique where a faster or cheaper process drafts likely output tokens and a larger model quickly verifies them, reducing generation time when the guesses are accepted.

destinations.title: Latency and throughput
destinations.def: Latency is how long a system takes to respond; throughput is how much work it can process over a period of time.
destinations.plain: A system can be fast for one user but bad at handling many users, or slower per request but capable of processing enormous volume.
destinations.why: Both affect user experience and economics, so AI infrastructure is optimized for more than raw model quality.

sections.title: Latency
sections.def: The delay between a request and the relevant response or completion.

sections.title: Throughput
sections.def: The amount of requests, tokens, or other work a system can process per unit of time.

destinations.title: Logging and monitoring
destinations.def: Recording what a system did and watching its behavior or condition so problems can be detected and investigated.
destinations.plain: Logging creates the records; monitoring watches signals and conditions over time.
destinations.why: Agents can take many hidden steps across tools, so organizations need evidence of what happened and alerts when behavior, cost, security, or reliability crosses a boundary.

sections.title: Logging
sections.def: Creating records of events, actions, inputs, outputs, tool calls, or changes for later inspection.

sections.title: Monitoring
sections.def: Continuously or repeatedly watching selected system signals to detect problems, changes, or threshold violations. It does not automatically imply the deeper system-internals focus of observability.

destinations.title: Long-horizon agents
destinations.def: AI work, systems, capabilities, or commitments that extend across a long period or many sequential steps rather than a short, one-shot interaction.
destinations.plain: “Long-horizon” means the relevant work has to stay coherent over time. For agents, that can mean hours-long coding or research jobs with many steps; Prompted also uses the phrase for longer-term capability work and computing commitments.
destinations.why: Longer horizons can make AI more useful and make infrastructure decisions more consequential, but they also give errors, costs, and weak assumptions more time to compound.

destinations.title: Model access and files
destinations.def: The ways users or organizations can obtain, control, host, or directly run AI models and their underlying files.
destinations.plain: Using a hosted chatbot is one access model; downloading model files and running them yourself is another. “Self-hosted” means you operate the serving environment.
destinations.why: Access determines who can use a model, where data flows, how much control the provider retains, and what happens if policy or geopolitics changes.

sections.title: Model access
sections.def: The ability or permission to use a model, through a product, API, trusted program, download, or other channel. It is distinct from security “access control” inside a system.

sections.title: Model files
sections.def: The downloadable technical files needed to run or inspect a model, especially its weights and configuration.

sections.title: Self-hosted
sections.def: Run by the user or organization on infrastructure it controls rather than solely through the original provider’s hosted service.

sections.title: Model repository
sections.def: A place for storing, versioning and sharing model files and associated documentation.
sections.plain: A model hub can host many such repositories and help people find or download models. Hosting files does not itself make a model open-source or grant unrestricted rights to use it.
sections.why: Control of a major model hub can affect how researchers and organizations obtain models, even when the files remain available elsewhere.

destinations.title: Model activations
destinations.def: The intermediate numerical signals produced inside a neural network as it processes an input.
destinations.plain: As information moves through the model’s layers, internal components switch on to different degrees. Those changing internal values are activations.
destinations.why: Researchers analyze activations to study what a model represents internally, and they also consume memory and compute during training and inference.

destinations.title: Model architectures
destinations.def: The structural design of a neural network: how its components are arranged and how information flows through them.
destinations.plain: Architecture is the model’s blueprint. Different designs can change how much compute is used, what the model can handle, and how efficiently it scales.
destinations.why: Architecture choices can produce major cost and performance differences even when two models have similar headline size.

sections.title: Dense model
sections.def: A model that generally uses the same full set of major parameters for each input step, rather than selecting only a subset of expert blocks.

sections.title: MoE
sections.def: Mixture of experts: an architecture with multiple expert subnetworks where only selected experts are activated for a given token or input, allowing very large total parameter counts without using all of them every time.

sections.title: Transformer
sections.def: The neural-network architecture built around attention mechanisms that became the foundation of most modern large language models and many multimodal models.

destinations.title: Model calls
destinations.def: An individual request sent to an AI model and the resulting model execution.
destinations.plain: If a workflow asks a model three separate questions, that usually creates three model calls, even if the user experiences it as one task.
destinations.why: Calls drive cost and latency. Agentic systems can make many hidden calls, so reducing unnecessary calls can materially improve unit economics.

destinations.title: Model documentation
destinations.def: Documents that explain how an AI model or system was built, evaluated, intended to be used, and limited.
destinations.plain: Think of these as technical disclosure documents. They can describe capabilities, benchmarks, safety testing, risks, and operating constraints.
destinations.why: Documentation lets users and reviewers judge a model on more than marketing claims, although the usefulness depends on what the developer actually discloses.

sections.title: Model documentation
sections.def: The broad category of technical and policy information published about a model.

sections.title: Model card
sections.def: A model-focused document describing intended use, performance, limitations, evaluations, and other relevant characteristics.

sections.title: System card
sections.def: A broader deployment-oriented safety document that can cover the model together with safeguards, product behavior, evaluations, and system-level risks.

destinations.title: Model governance
destinations.def: The policies, controls, ownership, and review processes used to manage an AI model across its lifecycle.
destinations.plain: Model governance answers who can approve a model, what tests it must pass, where it may run, how changes are tracked, and when it should be restricted or retired.
destinations.why: Organizations often use many models, so consistent governance matters for security, compliance, cost, and accountability.

destinations.title: Model Hardware Standard
destinations.def: A shared specification for letting AI agents discover, inspect, and operate programmable physical equipment through common commands and drivers.
destinations.plain: Instead of building a one-off integration for every microscope, robot arm, or lab device, the Model Hardware Standard aims to give agents a consistent way to connect to supported machines.
destinations.why: Standardization can make physical-agent systems easier to build, but it also creates a direct bridge from AI decisions to real equipment, making identity, permissions, and safety controls essential.

destinations.title: Model routing
destinations.def: Selecting which AI model should handle a request or step in a larger system.
destinations.plain: A router can send easy work to a cheap model, difficult reasoning to a stronger one, or specialized work to a model suited to that domain. A multi-model system is designed around several providers or models instead of one.
destinations.why: Routing can lower cost, improve reliability, and reduce dependence on any single provider, especially as model prices and access change quickly.

sections.title: Model router
sections.def: The software component that chooses which model receives a particular request.

sections.title: Model routing
sections.def: The broader process or strategy of directing work among models.

sections.title: Multi-model architecture
sections.def: A system intentionally designed to use multiple models, often with different roles or fallback paths.

sections.title: Model-neutral
sections.def: Designed so the surrounding product or workflow is not tightly dependent on one specific model provider or model family.

destinations.title: Model serving
destinations.def: The infrastructure and software that make a trained model available to receive requests and return outputs reliably at scale.
destinations.plain: Serving is the operational layer that loads the model onto hardware, accepts traffic, batches requests, manages memory, and sends answers back.
destinations.why: Efficient serving can materially lower cost and latency, so it is a major source of competitive advantage even when the model itself is unchanged.

sections.title: Model serving
sections.def: The overall process and infrastructure for running a model for users or applications.

sections.title: Serving layer
sections.def: The part of the system stack responsible for exposing and operating models for inference traffic.

destinations.title: Model training and pretraining
destinations.def: The process by which an AI model learns patterns from data by adjusting its internal parameters.
destinations.plain: Training is the learning phase. Pretraining is the broad, usually very large initial training stage before later specialization or fine-tuning.
destinations.why: Training determines much of a model’s capability and costs enormous amounts of data and compute at the frontier.

sections.title: Model training
sections.def: The general process of training an AI model; qualifying “training,” “train,” and “trained” references use this meaning when the surrounding text is about models rather than people.

sections.title: Pretraining
sections.def: The large initial training stage that teaches a model broad capabilities before task-specific adaptation or fine-tuning.

sections.title: Model checkpoint
sections.def: A saved version of an AI model at a particular point, including its learned weights and sometimes other information needed to resume training.
sections.plain: It is a recoverable snapshot, not necessarily a final release. A checkpoint containing only weights may be usable for inference without containing everything needed to continue training exactly.
sections.why: Intermediate checkpoints help researchers inspect how a model developed and reproduce or extend training work.

destinations.title: Model weights
destinations.def: The numerical values inside a trained model that encode what it learned from training.
destinations.plain: Weights are the learned settings of the network. If you have the model’s weights and the needed software and hardware, you can often run the model without asking the original provider for every inference.
destinations.why: Publishing or withholding weights changes how much control users have over a model and how easily it can be copied, modified, studied, or misused.

destinations.title: Multi-agent systems
destinations.def: AI systems that use more than one agent, with work divided or coordinated among them.
destinations.plain: Instead of one agent doing everything, a system can assign pieces to multiple agents that specialize, work in parallel, critique one another, or report to a lead agent.
destinations.why: Multi-agent designs can tackle larger tasks but create coordination, security, and accountability problems because actions and information pass among multiple autonomous components.

sections.title: Multi-agent system
sections.def: The overall system in which multiple AI agents interact or cooperate.

sections.title: Subagent
sections.def: A secondary agent assigned a narrower piece of work by another agent or orchestration layer.

destinations.title: Multimodal models
destinations.def: AI models that can work with more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio, video, or sensor data.
destinations.plain: A multimodal model does not live only in text. It can combine different kinds of input or produce different kinds of output.
destinations.why: Multimodality expands what AI can do in real products, from analyzing images and documents to voice, video, robotics, and screen-based agents.

destinations.title: Networking fabric
destinations.def: The high-speed network connecting large numbers of servers and accelerators so they can exchange data as one computing system.
destinations.plain: A training cluster is not useful if its chips cannot communicate quickly enough. The networking fabric is the web of links and switches that moves data among them.
destinations.why: At frontier scale, network failures or congestion can waste enormous amounts of expensive compute, so networking becomes a first-order AI infrastructure problem.

destinations.title: Observability and telemetry
destinations.def: Ways of understanding the internal state and behavior of a running system from the information it emits.
destinations.plain: Telemetry is the raw measurements and event data. Observability is the ability to use those signals to understand what is happening inside a complex system. Traceability is the ability to follow an action, output, or decision back through its relevant history.
destinations.why: Complex AI and agent systems can fail in hidden ways, so operators need more than logs: they need enough evidence to diagnose causes and reconstruct what happened.

sections.title: Observability
sections.def: The ability to infer and diagnose a system’s internal condition from outputs such as logs, metrics, traces, and events.

sections.title: Telemetry
sections.def: The measurements and event data a system automatically emits or sends for analysis, such as timing, errors, resource use, or tool activity.

sections.title: Traceability
sections.def: The ability to follow the origin and sequence of relevant steps, data, or decisions so an outcome can be reconstructed and attributed. It is not the same as general monitoring.

destinations.title: On-device AI
destinations.def: Running AI models directly on a user’s device, such as a phone, laptop, car, or wearable, instead of sending every request to a remote cloud server.
destinations.plain: The computation happens locally, at least for some tasks.
destinations.why: On-device AI can improve privacy, speed, offline use, and cloud cost, but device memory and power limit how large the model can be.

destinations.title: Open vs. closed AI models
destinations.def: Ways of describing how much of an AI model is publicly accessible versus controlled by its provider.
destinations.plain: “Open” and “closed” can refer to different things: access to the model or system, access to its trained weights, or the legal terms for using released materials. Prompted keeps those distinctions separate.
destinations.why: The difference determines whether users can download, inspect, modify, self-host, or redistribute a model and how much control the original provider retains.

sections.title: Open model
sections.def: A model or AI system made meaningfully available for outside use or inspection under relatively open terms. The label is broader and less precise than “open weight” or “open source,” so Prompted does not treat those terms as synonyms.

sections.title: Closed model
sections.def: A model or AI system whose operation or underlying artifacts remain controlled by the provider, typically accessed through a hosted product or API rather than freely downloaded.

sections.title: Proprietary model
sections.def: A model controlled under a company’s own non-open terms or intellectual property. A proprietary model is often closed, but the term emphasizes ownership and licensing rather than only technical access.

sections.title: Open weight
sections.def: A model whose trained weights are published for others to download. Open weights do not automatically mean open-source licensing, open training data, or permission to use the model for every purpose.

sections.title: Closed weight
sections.def: A model whose trained weights are not publicly released, even if people can use the model through a product or API.

destinations.title: Open-source AI licensing
destinations.def: The licensing terms that determine what others may legally do with released AI code, model files, or related materials.
destinations.plain: “Open source” is about source availability and legal permission to use, study, change, and redistribute material—not merely being able to call or download a model. Permissive licenses allow broad reuse with relatively few conditions.
destinations.why: Licensing determines whether developers can modify, redistribute, commercialize, or self-host released technology and what obligations follow.

sections.title: Open source
sections.def: Software or model-related material released with source access and a license granting rights to use, study, modify, and redistribute it. In AI, the phrase is often used loosely, so Prompted keeps it separate from “open weight.”

sections.title: Permissive license
sections.def: An open-source license that allows broad reuse, modification, and redistribution with relatively few ongoing restrictions.

sections.title: Apache 2.0
sections.def: A permissive open-source license that allows use, modification, and distribution and includes an express patent license and notice requirements.

sections.title: MIT license
sections.def: A short permissive open-source license allowing broad use, modification, distribution, and commercial use as long as the copyright and license notice is retained.

destinations.title: Orchestration
destinations.def: The coordination layer that manages how models, agents, tools, data, and workflow steps work together.
destinations.plain: Orchestration is the conductor: it decides what runs next, passes information between components, handles dependencies, and can retry or route work when something fails.
destinations.why: As AI products become multi-step and multi-model, the orchestration layer often determines reliability, cost, and how much autonomy the system actually has.

destinations.title: Parameters
destinations.def: The adjustable numerical values that determine how a model processes information; after training, the learned parameters contain much of what the model has learned.
destinations.plain: A model can have billions or trillions of parameters. In some architectures, only a subset is used for any one input.
destinations.why: Parameter counts are often used as a rough measure of model size and hardware needs, but they do not by themselves tell you how capable a model is.

sections.title: Parameter
sections.def: One learned numerical setting inside a model. “Parameters” is the plural form commonly used when describing model size.

sections.title: Active params
sections.def: The number of parameters actually used for a particular input or generation step, especially in mixture-of-experts models where the full parameter set is larger than the portion activated at once.

destinations.title: Persistent memory
destinations.def: Stored information that an AI system can carry forward beyond the current conversation or task.
destinations.plain: Instead of forgetting everything when one session ends, the system saves selected facts, preferences, prior work, or other state and retrieves it later.
destinations.why: Persistent memory can make agents more useful over time, but it also creates privacy, security, accuracy, and data-retention questions because old information can affect future actions.

destinations.title: Power units
destinations.def: Units used to measure power: a megawatt is one million watts, a gigawatt is one billion watts, and a terawatt is one trillion watts.
destinations.plain: MW, GW, and TW tell you the rate at which electricity is being produced or consumed—not how much energy was used over an entire period.
destinations.why: AI data centers are large enough that power requirements are increasingly discussed at utility and even national-grid scale, so these units help show the size of proposed projects.

sections.title: MW
sections.def: Megawatt: one million watts of power.

sections.title: Gigawatt
sections.def: One billion watts of power, equal to 1,000 megawatts; “GW” is the common abbreviation.

sections.title: Terawatt
sections.def: One trillion watts of power, equal to 1,000 gigawatts; “TW” is the common abbreviation.

destinations.title: Preemption
destinations.def: The legal principle that a higher level of law can override or displace a conflicting lower-level law.
destinations.plain: In Prompted, preemption means federal law may block a state AI law because the rules conflict or because the federal government has taken exclusive control of that area.
destinations.why: AI policy is developing at both federal and state levels, so preemption can determine which rules actually govern companies and whether a national framework replaces a patchwork of state requirements.

destinations.title: Price-performance
destinations.def: The amount of useful performance obtained for a given price.
destinations.plain: It asks not only “which model or chip is faster?” but “how much capability or throughput do I get for each dollar?”
destinations.why: Rapid improvements in price-performance can make previously uneconomic AI products viable even without a dramatic jump in absolute capability.

destinations.title: Private credit
destinations.def: Loans and other debt financing provided by non-bank private lenders rather than through public bond markets or traditional bank lending alone.
destinations.plain: Private-credit funds lend directly to companies or projects and negotiate the terms privately.
destinations.why: AI infrastructure is extremely capital-intensive, so private credit can help finance data centers and related projects while also shifting leverage and repayment risk onto borrowers and investors.

destinations.title: Prompt injection
destinations.def: Attacks that manipulate an AI system through instructions or context so it ignores intended rules or behaves in an unsafe or unauthorized way.
destinations.plain: Because models treat text as instructions and information, attackers can hide malicious directions in a user message, webpage, document, tool result, or other context. A jailbreak is usually a direct attempt to defeat safety restrictions.
destinations.why: Agents can read untrusted content and take real actions, so instruction-manipulation attacks can become security problems rather than merely strange chatbot outputs.

sections.title: Prompt injection
sections.def: An attack that places malicious instructions in content the model processes so those instructions compete with or override the system’s intended directions. The injected text may come directly from the user or indirectly from external content.

sections.title: Context injection
sections.def: Introducing deceptive or malicious material into the information supplied to an AI system so it changes the system’s reasoning or actions; the emphasis is on poisoning the supplied context, not necessarily on a direct user prompt.

sections.title: Jailbreak
sections.def: A prompt or interaction deliberately crafted to bypass a model’s safety restrictions or refusal behavior and elicit content or actions the system was intended to block.

destinations.title: Provenance and watermarking
destinations.def: Methods for establishing where digital content came from and, separately, for embedding or attaching signals that help identify its origin or processing history.
destinations.plain: Provenance is the history of a piece of content. Watermarking adds a detectable signal to content. C2PA is a technical standard for signed provenance records often presented as Content Credentials. These are related tools, not synonyms.
destinations.why: As AI-generated media becomes easier to create, origin evidence can help platforms, journalists, creators, and users judge what they are looking at—but no single method proves that content is true.

sections.title: Provenance
sections.def: Information about the origin and history of a piece of content, such as who created or edited it and what tools were used.

sections.title: Watermarking
sections.def: Adding a detectable signal or pattern to content so later systems can identify a source, generator, or other attribute. A watermark can be invisible and does not by itself provide the full edit history.

sections.title: C2PA
sections.def: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity: an open technical standard for cryptographically signed content-provenance records, commonly surfaced to users as Content Credentials.

destinations.title: RAG and agentic RAG
destinations.def: Retrieval-augmented generation: giving an AI model relevant information retrieved from outside its built-in training knowledge before it answers.
destinations.plain: Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training, RAG searches a document store, database, or other source and puts useful material into the model’s context. Agentic RAG lets an agent decide what to search, issue multiple retrieval steps, and adapt based on what it finds.
destinations.why: Retrieval can make answers more current, specific, and grounded in private data, but quality depends on finding the right information and using it correctly.

sections.title: RAG
sections.def: Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant external information, supply it to the model, then generate the answer using that added context.

sections.title: Agentic RAG
sections.def: RAG in which an AI agent actively plans and iterates the retrieval process—for example, choosing sources, reformulating searches, or retrieving again after inspecting earlier results.

destinations.title: Rate limits
destinations.def: A limit on how many requests, tokens, or other units of service a user or application may consume within a specified period.
destinations.plain: An API might allow only a certain number of calls per minute or tokens per day. Once the limit is reached, requests can be delayed or rejected until capacity resets.
destinations.why: Rate limits protect services from overload and abuse, but they can also constrain how quickly AI products and agents can operate at scale.

destinations.title: Reasoning models
destinations.def: An AI model designed or trained to work through difficult problems using intermediate reasoning or deliberation rather than only producing an immediate answer or action.
destinations.plain: A reasoning model is built to work through a problem before answering or acting. Some use extra computation at inference time; others are specialized for reasoning in domains such as math, science, driving, or robotics.
destinations.why: Reasoning models can improve performance on difficult multi-step tasks, though the extra deliberation can cost more time or compute. “Reasoning model” is the model category; “AI reasoning” is the broader behavior or capability.

destinations.title: Red teaming and pre-release testing
destinations.def: Deliberate testing intended to find failures, vulnerabilities, or dangerous capabilities before or around release.
destinations.plain: Red teaming means actively trying to break the system from an adversary’s point of view. Pre-release testing is the broader set of checks performed before public or wider deployment.
destinations.why: Finding problems before release gives developers a chance to fix, restrict, or document them before real users and attackers discover them.

sections.title: Red teaming
sections.def: Adversarial testing in which evaluators intentionally try to cause failures, bypass safeguards, expose vulnerabilities, or discover dangerous behavior.

sections.title: Pre-release testing
sections.def: The broader testing performed before a model or product is made generally available; it can include red teaming, capability evals, safety tests, and ordinary quality assurance.

destinations.title: Reinforcement learning
destinations.def: Reinforcement learning: a training method in which a system learns to favor actions or outputs that receive higher reward signals.
destinations.plain: The model tries behavior, receives feedback about what was better or worse, and training pushes it toward behavior that earns more reward.
destinations.why: RL is widely used to shape model behavior after pretraining and to improve reasoning or agent performance, but the result depends heavily on what the reward actually measures.

destinations.title: Reproducibility
destinations.def: The ability to repeat or recreate a result, process, or capability from sufficiently documented methods, data, settings, computing resources, and other relevant conditions.
destinations.plain: Reproducibility means someone can see how work was produced and rerun or rebuild it closely enough to check whether the same result or capability holds. A reproducibility trail records the models, data, tools, settings, steps, and human changes needed to reconstruct the work.
destinations.why: Prompted uses reproducibility for both research claims and AI-building or research workflows. It helps distinguish durable, auditable capability from a one-off result that may depend on a hidden setup, specially chosen problem, or undocumented process.

destinations.title: Run rate
destinations.def: An annualized or otherwise standardized estimate based on the current pace of a financial metric.
destinations.plain: If a company is producing $100 million of revenue per month, a simple annual revenue run rate would be about $1.2 billion—even if it has not actually earned that amount over a full year.
destinations.why: Fast-growing AI companies often cite run rates because recent performance can differ sharply from trailing-year totals, but run rate is an extrapolation, not the same as audited full-year results.

destinations.title: S-1 filings
destinations.def: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission registration statement commonly filed by a company preparing an initial public offering of securities.
destinations.plain: An S-1 gives prospective investors a detailed look at the business, including financial statements, risks, ownership, and how the offering is structured.
destinations.why: For AI companies heading toward public markets, an S-1 can reveal economics and risks that private-company announcements do not.

sections.title: S-1
sections.def: Form S-1, the SEC registration statement widely used for a U.S. company’s initial public offering and related public disclosure.

destinations.title: Safety cases
destinations.def: The argument and evidence for why a model, system, or safety decision is considered safe enough for a particular use or level of access.
destinations.plain: A safety case answers: “Why should we believe this is safe enough?” It can be a formal, structured assurance case, but Prompted also uses the phrase more broadly for the reasoning behind a safety decision, such as withholding access to a powerful model.
destinations.why: Safety claims are more useful when readers can see the evidence, assumptions, and tradeoffs behind them rather than only being told that a system was “tested” or “safe.”

destinations.title: Sandboxing
destinations.def: Isolating code or an AI system inside a restricted execution environment so mistakes or malicious behavior cannot freely affect the surrounding computer or network.
destinations.plain: A sandbox is the fenced area. The runtime is the environment in which the code actually executes; a runtime can be sandboxed by limiting files, network access, processes, privileges, and other capabilities.
destinations.why: Coding agents and tool-using models can execute untrusted or mistaken actions, so containment at runtime limits the damage if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Sandbox
sections.def: A deliberately isolated environment with restricted access to the host system, network, files, or other resources.

sections.title: Runtime
sections.def: The software environment in which code or an agent’s actions are actually executed. A runtime is not automatically a sandbox; it becomes one only when meaningful isolation and restrictions are imposed.

destinations.title: Small modular reactors
destinations.def: Small modular reactor: a nuclear reactor designed with a smaller output and modular construction approach than a conventional large nuclear power plant.
destinations.plain: Instead of building one enormous reactor entirely on site, SMR designs aim to use standardized modules that can be manufactured and deployed in smaller increments.
destinations.why: AI data centers need large, steady supplies of electricity, so technology companies and utilities are exploring SMRs as one possible long-term power source.

destinations.title: Startup valuations
destinations.def: Two ways of valuing a startup around a financing round: pre-money is the company’s value immediately before the new investment, and post-money is the value immediately after it.
destinations.plain: If investors put $20 million into a company at an $80 million pre-money valuation, the simple post-money valuation is $100 million.
destinations.why: The distinction determines what ownership percentage new money buys and prevents headline funding numbers from being confused with the company’s value before the round.

sections.title: Pre-money
sections.def: The agreed value of a company immediately before a new financing is added.

sections.title: Post-money
