sections.def: The company’s value immediately after the new financing is added; in the simplest case, pre-money valuation plus the new investment.

destinations.title: Stock warrants
destinations.def: A financial instrument giving its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy a company’s stock at specified terms before the warrant expires.
destinations.plain: A warrant can become valuable if the company’s share price rises above the price at which the holder is allowed to buy. Companies sometimes issue warrants as part of financing or strategic agreements.
destinations.why: In AI deals, warrants can give a partner future equity upside without being the same thing as buying those shares immediately.

destinations.title: System prompts
destinations.def: Hidden or higher-priority instructions supplied by the AI application to guide a model’s behavior before the user’s request is processed.
destinations.plain: The system prompt tells the model its role, rules, available tools, formatting expectations, and other operating instructions. Users usually interact beneath that instruction layer.
destinations.why: System prompts shape behavior but are not a complete security boundary: malicious input, model limitations, or tool permissions can still create failures.

destinations.title: Systems integrators
destinations.def: A company that combines software, hardware, data, and business processes from multiple vendors into a working system for a customer.
destinations.plain: A systems integrator does the messy implementation work: connecting products to existing enterprise systems, customizing workflows, migrating data, and making the pieces operate together.
destinations.why: Enterprise AI adoption often depends less on having access to a model than on integrating it safely into real operations, so integrators can capture substantial value.

destinations.title: Threat models
destinations.def: A structured description of what must be protected, who or what might attack or fail, how harm could occur, and which defenses are expected to stop it.
destinations.plain: A threat model asks: what are the valuable assets, what can an attacker or faulty system do, through which paths, and what happens if defenses fail?
destinations.why: AI agents create new attack paths through tools, credentials, data, and autonomous actions, so an explicit threat model helps teams secure the real system rather than only the model.

destinations.title: Tokenizers
destinations.def: The component that converts text or other inputs into the discrete units a model processes, and converts generated units back into readable form.
destinations.plain: Models do not usually read text one character or one word at a time. A tokenizer breaks it into tokens—often pieces of words, punctuation, or other patterns—according to a fixed vocabulary.
destinations.why: Tokenization affects context-window usage, API billing, multilingual efficiency, and how text is represented to the model.

destinations.title: Tokens
destinations.def: A token is one of the discrete units an AI model processes when reading or generating content.
destinations.plain: Tokens are often shorter than a word and can be pieces of words, punctuation, numbers, or other encoded units. Input tokens go into the model; output tokens are generated by it.
destinations.why: Model pricing and context limits are commonly measured in tokens, so token counts directly affect cost, latency, and how much material fits in one request.

sections.title: Token
sections.def: The general unit processed by a model; “tokens” is the plural form commonly used in pricing, context, and throughput discussions.

sections.title: Input token
sections.def: A token supplied to the model as part of the prompt, conversation, retrieved context, tool results, or other input.

sections.title: Output token
sections.def: A token generated by the model in its response or intermediate output.

destinations.title: Tool use
destinations.def: Allowing an AI model to invoke external software capabilities instead of only producing text.
destinations.plain: A tool might search the web, query a database, send a message, run code, or control another application. Function calling is a structured mechanism that lets the model choose a predefined function and provide the arguments for it.
destinations.why: Tool access turns models into agents that can affect real systems, so capability grows together with the need for permissions, validation, and human controls.

sections.title: Tool use
sections.def: The broader ability of an AI system to select and use external tools or actions.

sections.title: Function calling
sections.def: A structured interface where the model requests that a named function be invoked with specified arguments; the surrounding application executes it and returns the result.

destinations.title: TPU
destinations.def: Tensor Processing Unit: Google’s custom accelerator hardware designed for machine-learning workloads.
destinations.plain: A TPU is an alternative to GPUs for many AI computations, with hardware and software optimized around large tensor operations used by neural networks.
destinations.why: TPUs give Google a major in-house source of AI compute and can affect the cost, capacity, and competitive economics of training and serving models.

destinations.title: Training clusters
destinations.def: A large group of interconnected computers and AI accelerators operated together to train a model.
destinations.plain: Frontier training divides an enormous learning job across many chips. The cluster includes the accelerators, servers, networking, storage, and software that keep that distributed work synchronized.
destinations.why: Training clusters require huge capital, power, and engineering effort, making their scale a useful signal of frontier-model investment.

destinations.title: Training data and recipes
destinations.def: The information used to teach a model and the detailed procedure used to turn that information into a trained model.
destinations.plain: Training data is what the model learns from. A training recipe is how the developer prepares that data and combines it with objectives, optimization settings, schedules, filtering, and other choices during training.
destinations.why: Two teams can use similar data and hardware yet get different models because the recipe differs; both data quality and training method affect capability, bias, safety, and reproducibility.

sections.title: Training data
sections.def: The examples, text, images, audio, code, or other information used as input to the model-learning process.

sections.title: Training recipes
sections.def: The collection of training procedures and choices—such as data mixing, objectives, optimization settings, schedules, and post-training steps—that determine how a model is trained.

destinations.title: Trust layers
destinations.def: A layer of controls, evidence, and governance intended to make an AI system’s outputs and actions more trustworthy and manageable.
destinations.plain: A trust layer sits around or between AI components and can provide things such as authoritative data, citations, identity, permissions, policy checks, evaluation, logging, or governance. The exact components depend on the product.
destinations.why: Enterprises often need a dependable control layer around models and agents before they can use them in sensitive workflows, especially when multiple models and data sources are involved.

destinations.title: Unit economics
destinations.def: The revenue, direct cost, and profit associated with one unit of a product or transaction.
destinations.plain: Unit economics asks whether each customer, task, API call, or other unit makes economic sense before overhead and scale effects are considered.
destinations.why: AI products can have unusually high variable compute costs, so strong growth does not guarantee a sustainable business if each additional unit loses money.

destinations.title: Vulnerabilities and exploits
destinations.def: Security weaknesses and the methods used to take advantage of them.
destinations.plain: A vulnerability is the flaw. A zero-day is a flaw defenders have essentially no advance time to patch. An exploit is the technique or code that uses a flaw; to exploit a vulnerability means to use that weakness to cause unintended behavior. Remote code execution lets an attacker run code on another machine, while a supply-chain attack reaches victims through a trusted upstream dependency, vendor, build, or update path.
destinations.why: AI systems both create new security surfaces and increasingly help defenders and attackers find or use software flaws, so these distinctions matter when judging the severity of a cyber story.

sections.title: Vulnerability
sections.def: A weakness in software, hardware, configuration, or design that can be abused or can cause a security failure.

sections.title: Zero-day vulnerability
sections.def: A security flaw for which defenders have no effective fix when exploitation becomes possible or public. “Zero-day” means they effectively had zero advance patching time.

sections.title: Exploit
sections.def: An exploit is code, a technique, or a sequence of actions that takes advantage of a vulnerability. As a verb, to exploit a flaw means to use that weakness to produce an unintended effect.

sections.title: Remote code exec
sections.def: Remote code execution (RCE): a flaw or attack that lets someone run code on another machine from a remote position.

sections.title: Supply-chain attack
sections.def: An attack that compromises a trusted vendor, dependency, build process, update mechanism, or other upstream component so the compromise reaches downstream users or systems.

destinations.title: Preliminary injunction
destinations.def: A temporary court order issued while a case is pending that requires or prohibits specified conduct before a final decision.
destinations.plain: It can preserve the situation or prevent harm while the dispute is litigated. Granting or denying one is not the same as a final ruling on the underlying claim.
destinations.why: A law remaining in force after a preliminary injunction is denied does not mean the court has finally upheld that law.
